claims.claim: Cyprian of Carthage was bishop of Carthage from 248/249 until his martyrdom in 258.
Cyprian was born around 200 CE in Carthage and was educated in law and rhetoric before converting to Christianity about 246.

On the Lord's Prayer was composed early in Cyprian's episcopate, during a period when the African Church had enjoyed nearly thirty years of peace that had slackened zeal and discipline among its members.
The treatise was addressed to Cyprian's congregation, whom he calls 'beloved brethren' throughout the work.
The work imitates Tertullian's earlier Book on Prayer in its three-part structure: the excellence of the Lord's Prayer, explanation of its seven chief clauses, and the conditions of prayer.

The treatise was written to provide instruction on proper prayer at a time when many Christians needed spiritual guidance, with Cyprian emphasizing that to pray otherwise than Christ taught is not ignorance alone but also sin.
The work survives through manuscript tradition and was regarded as the recognized standard treatise on the Lord's Prayer by the early Church.
St. Hilary of Poitiers, writing in 354, considered himself relieved from commenting on the Lord's Prayer in his Matthew commentary, preferring to send readers to Cyprian's well-known book instead.

The treatise preserves Cyprian's Old Latin text of the Lord's Prayer, which read 'Thy will be done in heaven and in earth' rather than 'as in heaven so in earth,' and 'Allow us not to be led into temptation' rather than 'Lead us not into temptation.'
